name: Water-assisted liposuction (BodyJet)

lead: Water-assisted liposuction uses a jet of fluid to loosen fat while it is suctioned out, for a leaner body contour. BodyJet is a branded system. It is also used to collect fat for transfer to other areas such as the breast.

A fan-shaped water jet through the cannula delivers fluid and anesthetic and detaches fat, which is then aspirated. Published research is concentrated in fat-grafting and tissue-quality studies, such as case series and lab comparisons, rather than in contouring outcomes.

paras: It is a surgical procedure done by a surgeon, usually with compression garments afterwards and a recovery of several weeks. The contour change shows once swelling settles.
Risks are those of liposuction generally, including pain, bruising, contour irregularity, infection, bleeding, clots and rare deaths. No device-specific safety data were identified.

angle.text: Water-assisted liposuction, including the BodyJet system, is used for fat removal and body contouring. A water jet loosens fat before it is aspirated, and the leaner contour shows after healing. Research is mainly on fat harvesting.

lead: Water-assisted liposuction (WAL), also called water-jet-assisted liposuction, is a liposuction technique in which a fan-shaped jet of fluid is delivered through the cannula to loosen fat and infiltrate anesthetic while the fat is aspirated. BodyJet is a commercial system for the method.[1]

The technique is used for body contouring and for harvesting fat for transfer to other areas such as the breast. Published research on the method is concentrated in fat-grafting and tissue-quality studies rather than in appearance outcomes of contouring.[2][3][4][5]
infobox: Fan-shaped water jet delivering fluid while fat is aspirated
Body contouring, fat harvesting for grafting

paras: Wikipedia lists water-jet-assisted liposuction among the main liposuction variants, describing a fan-shaped water jet that delivers anesthetic and assists fat removal, with BodyJet as an example.[1]

A 2010 German report described the BEAULI method, a water-jet-based approach to collecting large amounts of fat for transplantation, evaluated in a prospective clinical study of 85 patients.[2] A later series of 96 breast augmentations with the BEAULI technique was published in 2013.[6]

A 2017 case series of 12 breast reconstructions used fat grafting performed with either the Coleman technique or the BodyJet system.[3] A 2017 comparison of four commercial lipotransfer protocols examined how processed fat behaved in an animal model.[4]

Evidence is mainly surgical case series and laboratory comparisons. A 2015 study found that mesenchymal stem cells isolated after manual or water-jet-assisted liposuction displayed similar properties.[5] A 2007 randomized trial of postoperative pain compared a power water-assisted device with traditional liposuction.[7] No large randomized trials of contouring outcomes specific to BodyJet were identified.

timeline.event: German surgeons develop the BEAULI water-jet fat-harvesting method.[2]
